paragraphs: In the autumn of Yuanxing’s second year, a battered cart reached the gates of Chang’an. Hemp rope bound its axle, two spokes were missing, and a small bronze casket rested in the bed. Half a broken seal had been set into its lid. Wind had split the driver’s skin and crusted his lips with blood. Once beneath the gate, he clasped the casket to his chest, afraid someone might reach out and take it.

He said he came from Liyang. The soldiers guarding grain in the city had been replaced three times. Rice borrowed from the various households had never been repaid, and only one granary remained. The third army to arrive had demanded ferryboats, claiming orders from Jiankang to put down the rebellion, and had detained boat owners who could not provide them. Liyang’s governor no longer dared issue a document under his seal, so several village headmen and the garrison’s staff officer had jointly signed a roll of hemp paper. Near the Huai they had feared the document might be taken as a surrender to Qin. They had a craftsman smash half of the official seal, leaving just enough to show that the letter was no bandit forgery.
A Secretariat examiner looked first at the casket, then at the man. “What do you want?”
“Grain. And if you have soldiers, send some to defend the city.”
“Under whose authority is the city?”
“We still use the Jin reign calendar.”
“If Qin soldiers defend it, whose commands are they to obey?”

The traveler’s throat was too dry to speak. He bowed his head and drank half a bowl of warm water before answering. “Whichever army is willing to stay without taking our grain, we will listen to that army first.”

The examiner did not enter this answer in the record. Under Qin law, an appeal for help from civilians was not the same as stationing troops across a national border. Without a governor’s seal and complete, verified travel papers, the joint signatures of several hundred people could not justify a military order. He lodged the man from Liyang in the post station and sent junior clerks to the frontier garrisons to verify how many granaries, households, and defenders the city actually had.

The envoy who entered the city the following day was neatly dressed and carried Jin government documents wrapped against the rain. His leader, Lu Xunli, came from a collateral branch of the Lu clan of Kuaiji. Having studied in Jiankang as a young man, he could still invoke the dignified language of Jin court ceremony. Huan Xuan, he said, had seized control of the government offices, and the southern ancestral temples were in danger. He asked Qin to send troops to help Jin suppress the rebellion. Before he had finished, he spread his conditions across the table: the ancestral temples and imperial tombs must not be destroyed; dress, rites, and customs must not be forcibly changed; the estates of those who had not supported the rebellion must be protected; and local officers must not all be replaced by northerners.
A minister asked, “And after the troops enter Jiankang?”
“Each side returns to its own territory.”
“If the city remains divided, who will guard it after they leave?”
“That is for the Jin people to decide,” Lu Xunli replied.

The minister asked nothing more. He knew what this scholar sought: the cutting edge of a northern army, while the south retained the name and legitimacy of its own state. The wish was understandable. What was difficult was to say who would furnish grain and boats, and pay for the dead, once that army entered the south. Even Lu Xunli could produce no sealed promise of repayment.

The third party arrived at midnight. A soldier lowered a lamp from the battlement and saw more than twenty people standing in the frosty dew: old men, women, and two who had once worn armor. They had sold every iron plate, leaving only a chafed mark around the neck. They carried a white cloth densely covered with palm prints of every size. The leader, an elder surnamed Zhou, held a sheet folded many times over. Its message read: Neither Qin nor Jin matters. We ask only that the fighting stop.

The soldiers told them to wait until dawn. Suddenly one woman loosened the cloth bundle on her back, crouched at the foot of the wall, and fell silent. The child in her arms had died on the road. The night curfew was still in force, but a side wicket opened. The guards cleared a sheltered space for them just within the wall. The next day, the recording official wrote “Opening the gate in breach of regulations”

at the head of the register, and entered the dead child’s name below it. He asked Elder Zhou where they wished troops sent. The old man answered: wherever soldiers were taking people’s grain. The official reminded him that Qin troops, too, would have to eat once they crossed the border. Zhou looked at the hot porridge in his hands. “Then what matters is whether they eat grain that belongs to them or grain they have stolen.”

Plane-tree leaves covered the ground in Chang’an on the day all three parties were summoned to a side hall. The hems of the Liyang envoy’s shoes were coming unstitched. Lu Xunli’s attendants spread a cushion for their master. Elder Zhou simply sat on the floor and first asked whether the women and children could be fed. As officials passed messages back and forth, the differences gradually became clear: one group wanted its city defended; another wanted northern soldiers to restore Jin rule; the third cared little who ruled any city, only that tomorrow no one would come to slaughter their pigs, lead away their cattle, or reap the last stalks of their crops.

Fu Jian listened for a long time from behind a curtain. His old ministers, seeing the dark rings beneath his eyes, urged him not to sit too long. Since his grave illness years earlier, he had kept his hours according to his physicians’ instructions. Each autumn his knees ached, and after court he often needed a walking stick. Now he ordered the curtain removed so the three groups from the south could look up and see him.

The Liyang envoy bowed first. Lu Xunli paid the respects due from a Jin minister without acknowledging the Qin ruler as Son of Heaven. Elder Zhou had no time for ceremony: he still gripped a piece of dried cake intended for his grandson. Fu Jian placed the three petitions side by side. The sheets differed in length, the handwriting in refinement. The years had at last taught him to distinguish what people asked for from what they were willing to say aloud. Their need for help was genuine, and so were their quarrels with one another. On the strength of these three documents alone, he could not claim that the south had given him its consent.

At the court council, veteran commanders urged him to seize the moment and cross the Huai. Huan Xuan was powerful but had not yet brought every regional garrison under his hand. Liu Laozhi had lost the allegiance of the Northern Garrison’s rank and file, and the camps around Jingkou distrusted one another. If Qin waited another two years, the south might produce a leader capable of resisting a northern army.

Fu Pi’s gaze rested on the map of the Jiang–Huai lands. Since the Xiangyang campaign, he had ceased to assume that greater numbers alone could guarantee victory. He proposed first securing several crossings on the southern shore and sheltering the counties that had appealed for aid behind the army. Then he pointed out the cost. If Qin sent only grain, Huan Xuan’s men would sooner or later seize it. If it sent troops, every new place held would require rations, replacement garrisons, and a fleet of boats. Any of those not supplied by Qin would have to be paid for by the local people.

Fu Rong ordered the campaign expense accounts opened. They recorded the money and grain spent on relief payments, road repairs, and withdrawal after the forces had assembled at the Fei River twenty years earlier. The paper had yellowed; the fresh cuts in the counting rods remained distinct. “A hundred and fifty thousand men came to the Fei River then,” he said. “We never fought a great battle with the Jin army, yet men still fell sick or starved on the march home, and families lost everything they owned. This time we propose to cross the Huai into a country in civil war. Before we march, we must ask whose roads our carts will use and whose landings will take our boats.”

Murong Chui sat among the generals, his back no longer as straight as in his youth. Someone argued that Qin’s military registers were now complete enough for it to absorb the south. Murong Chui did not dispute the claim directly. He cited an old relief case from the floods at Ye: after more than a decade of incorporating former Yan land records, powerful families could still use a single old deed to hold newly registered citizens in bondage. The south was thick with fortified estates and divided by mountains and rivers. If Qin troops arrived and immediately began pulling down houses and surveying fields, half a month would be enough to drive even villagers inclined to wait and see into the enemy camp.

Fu Hong added a blank sheet to the table. First, he proposed, they must draft a compact governing the army: a city that requested assistance must be distinguished from a city under occupation; one city’s request must not automatically count as the surrender of neighboring counties; the army must bring its own rations; civilian grain purchased by the army must be covered by receipts, with named officials responsible for prices and repayment; troops who laid down their arms must not be killed without lawful process; and old Jin government documents could not be swept aside overnight.

A general laughed that they had not yet crossed the river and were already tying ropes around their own soldiers. Fu Jian asked what an officer would report if hungry Qin soldiers took three shi of grain from a civilian. The general said it could be entered as military provisions. Fu Jian asked again how a woman of the city was supposed to know when she would be paid. For a moment the general had no answer.

“You speak of armies advancing and withdrawing,” said Fu Jian. “She sees only that her sacks of grain have vanished. If an order cannot be explained to a village woman, so that she knows where to complain when a soldier breaks it, what use is the punishment you threaten?”

Lu Xunli was summoned to inspect the draft compact. He drew a line through a clause concerning Jin’s ancestral temples. “Not to destroy them for the time being,” he said, was far too weak; the document must say “protect.” He also asked whether, once Huan Xuan was defeated, Qin would withdraw from every crossing. Fu Jian refused to promise that. He stated plainly that Qin still intended to unite all under Heaven. Lu Xunli was silent for a long while, then wrote his name in the column marked “Read, but not agreed in full.”

Fu Jian did not press him. He remembered how Wang Meng had urged him, years ago, to proceed slowly against the south. Back then he had believed that once southerners saw Qin administration with their own eyes, they would willingly submit. Twenty years of travel between the north and south had followed. Refugees, merchants, and healers crossed the river constantly. What could change the mind of a single household did not necessarily change the mind of an entire country. Across the river lay ancestral graves, old grievances, and people who would rather be free to make their own mistakes.

When the council reached the assessment of land taxes, several ministers proposed taking advantage of the campaign to survey every estate. Lu Xunli objected immediately. A land-requisition decree, he said, would shut the fortified gates of people who might otherwise welcome the army. He admitted that the powerful had swallowed many smaller holdings, but asked that private seizure during the war first be prohibited, and that northern and southern officials jointly examine old deeds afterward. For three years no land already under cultivation should be confiscated in the name of surveying it. Fu Rong thought three years too long; Fu Hong insisted on specifying how actual cultivation would be proved. The discussion lasted from afternoon into dusk.

By the time Elder Zhou was led to the table, he was nearly asleep. A palace attendant read him the important clauses of the draft. He asked only three questions: could soldiers quarter themselves in private houses; would grain purchases be paid for on the spot; and if someone was killed, would there be a judgment? Fu Jian had the legal officers address each point. He also ordered notices posted at gates, grain depots, and army camps, and allowed people to submit complaints in an intake register. Zhou ran his fingers along the paper’s edge and asked what happened if an official refused to receive a complaint. Fu Jian answered that it could be sent to an inspector. The elder said his village was far from the city. Who could afford to take it there?

Several officials looked uncomfortable. Fu Hong promptly amended the clause. A point for receiving petitions would be established every twenty li in the army’s jurisdiction; people would not first have to pass through three government offices. Literate local residents could write on their behalf, and the receiving official must sign the register each day. This required more clerks and more transport labor. The accounts officer frowned and wrote down the cost on the spot. Everyone knew the arrangement might not be carried out everywhere. At least someone had taken the trouble to calculate what it would cost.

On the day the Compact for Crossing the River was finalized, the relay horses at Chang’an’s eastern gate were changed four times. Copies went to frontier commands, provinces, and all three southern delegations. The first force was limited to fifty thousand. Troops could not requisition households on their own authority, and the joint signatures of one southern community could not make neighboring counties surrendered territory. Fu Hong remained in Chang’an; Fu Rong took charge of grain supply and roads; Murong Chui commanded the vanguard. Fu Jian did not proclaim that the south now belonged to Qin, nor did he call the petitioners official envoys of the Jin court.

Fearing that his granary would be empty before the troops arrived, the Liyang envoy departed first with a bundle of grain vouchers. Lu Xunli rolled the compact into a narrow tube and tucked it inside his robe, saying he could not yet promise anything for his clan. Elder Zhou asked for two copies: one to leave with the villagers, the other to show county officials along the road. He buried the child who had died outside Chang’an’s gate on a barren hill west of the city. Only after borrowing a spade and patting the new earth firm with his own hands did he board the relay carriage south.

When the Qin army marched from Luoyang through Shouyang toward the south, the autumn rain was relentless. North of the Huai, troops prepared pontoon bridges, boats, and camp roads. From the southern bank came contradictory messages: Liyang still begged for aid, another city now asked only for grain, and a fortified estate that had once welcomed Qin abruptly barred its gates. Wooden tablets setting out the compact were carried to several crossings in small boats. Some on the shore read them carefully. Others threw stones and cursed Qin’s pretended benevolence. Until the order came, the vanguard did not cross the border.

Since returning south from Jiankang, Zhu Xu had remained in Jin territory. He had audited Qin grain with Liu Yu; later, after speaking openly of refugees’ sufferings, he came under surveillance by officials of Huan Xuan’s administration. Hearing Liyang’s appeal for troops, he offered to mediate at the Huai. He took no Qin seal, nor did he carry edicts on Huan Xuan’s behalf. Murong Chui allowed him, as the former defender of Xiangyang, to take a boat to midstream and first observe the disposition of the forces on the southern bank.

Winter floodwater had yet to recede completely. Liu Yu drew up a Northern Garrison detachment along the shallows, with grain wagons collected from nearby villages behind him. Seeing Zhu Xu’s boat pause in midstream, he ordered the strings removed from the crossbows within range and stood at the water’s edge to wait. The two spoke across a stretch of river. Those on shore could not clearly hear their words.

Zhu Xu told him that Liyang truly had appealed for Qin to defend it and that Jiankang had sent no help. Could the villagers who asked for troops, Liu Yu inquired, decide the fate of all the other southern provinces and counties? No, Zhu Xu said. Then who would bear responsibility if Qin did not come and the people of Liyang failed to survive the winter? To that Zhu Xu had no answer either.
“I will let the grain boats through,” Liu Yu said at last. “The soldiers must wait on the bank.”

Zhu Xu heard him plainly. Years earlier, Liu Yu had faced charges for allowing Qin grain into Xuyi. Now he was willing to bear the same suspicion again, yet he drew a line between grain and soldiers. Zhu Xu looked at the waterlogged battle flag beside Liu Yu’s feet and felt that the young officer before him was quite unlike the one who had once demanded his arrears of pay at Jingkou.
“Can you hold the line?”
Liu Yu glanced at the uneven stockades behind him. “Perhaps not. Even if we cannot, someone must stand the first night.”

Zhu Xu returned to the northern bank and reported their exchange without embellishment. Fu Jian did not order an advance at once. He had the reports on the authenticity of the requests from the southern counties laid beside Lu Xunli’s proposed conditions for halting the army. Fifty thousand troops were already north of the Huai, their camps waiting for boats, their banners stretched together through the rain. Fu Jian asked Fu Rong how many ten-day periods the remaining grain supplies would last. Then he asked Murong Chui how many days it would take to drive back Liu Yu without harming the villagers. Breaking the force in front of them would not be difficult, the old general replied, but that did not mean the south beyond it would open its gates.

At dusk Fu Jian left his command tent and walked slowly along the Huai to the highest lookout. In the distance, a tributary of the Fei River disappeared into rain and mist. He dimly remembered the bitter wind on his first arrival in this region twenty years earlier. The officers awaited his decision on whether to build the bridge that night. He ordered the army to remain within its established camp boundaries, three counties’ grain boats to pass first, and the frontier commands to guard the border markers strictly.
“I intend to see the Fei River country for myself,” he told Fu Rong.

The order to march went down the line. Soldiers kept sharpening their blades; boatmen went on mending their cables. No cheers rose from the banks. A little boat from the south nosed toward shore. A woman on board hugged a sack of damp rice. All she knew was that tonight she could enter the camp to have her dressings changed. She knew nothing of the seals Qin and Jin had pressed upon the papers that would decide her journey home.
